title: الماضي التام / Past Perfect
bridge: In Spanish, the past perfect is formed with the auxiliary 'haber' in the imperfect plus the past participle (había comido). In Arabic, this tense does not exist as a specific verbal form; it is expressed with the particle 'قَد' (already) attached to the past verb, or through constructions with 'كَانَ' (to be in the past) plus another past verb. The key is that in Arabic, anteriority is marked with lexical elements (such as 'قَبْلَ' = before) or by combining tenses, not with a specific verbal morpheme. For Spanish speakers, the most challenging aspect is getting used to the fact that there is no special conjugation, but rather analytical structures are used.
rule:
In Arabic, the past of the past (past perfect) is expressed in several ways:

1. **With 'كَانَ' in the past + past verb**: The most common structure is using the verb 'كَانَ' (kāna, 'to be') in its past conjugation, followed by the main verb also in the past. Example: 'كَانَ قَدْ أَكَلَ' (kāna qad ʼakala, 'he had eaten'). Literally: 'he was (and) already ate'. Usually, 'قَدْ' (qad) is added to emphasize anteriority.

2. **With the particle 'قَدْ' (qad)**: Placed before a past verb, it indicates that the action had already occurred in relation to another past action. Example: 'لَمَّا وَصَلْتُ، كَانَ قَدْ غَادَرَ' (when I arrived, he had already left).

3. **With temporal particles**: 'قَبْلَ' (before) + noun or verb, or 'بَعْدَ أَنْ' (after) + past verb, to clarify the sequence.

4. **In sentences with 'لَوْ' (if) for unreal conditionals**: 'لَوْ كَانَ قَدْ دَرَسَ، لَنَجَحَ' (if he had studied, he would have passed). Here, 'كَانَ' + 'قَدْ' + past is used.

**Conjugation of 'كَانَ' in the past (for reference):**
- أنا كُنْتُ (ʼanā kuntu) = I was
- أنتَ كُنْتَ (ʼanta kunta) = you (masc.) were
- هو كَانَ (huwa kāna) = he was
- هي كَانَتْ (hiya kānat) = she was
- نحن كُنَّا (naḥnu kunnā) = we were
- أنتم كُنْتُمْ (ʼantum kuntum) = you (pl.) were
- هم كَانُوا (hum kānū) = they were

**Typical use**: To narrate past events where one occurs before another. In Arabic, the order of verbs (perfect/imperfect) can also indicate sequence, but with 'كَانَ' it is more explicit.

concept_examples.text: كَانَ قَدْ أَكَلَ الطَّعَامَ قَبْلَ أَنْ تَصِلَ.
concept_examples.translation: He had eaten the food before you arrived.
concept_examples.phonetic: kāna qad ʼakala aṭ-ṭaʿāma qabla ʼan taṣila.

concept_examples.text: لَمَّا ذَهَبْتُ إِلَى البَيْتِ، كَانَتْ قَدْ خَرَجَتْ.
concept_examples.translation: When I went home, she had already left.
concept_examples.phonetic: lammā ḏahabtu ʼilā l-bayti, kānat qad ḫarajat.

concept_examples.text: لَوْ كَانَ قَدْ دَرَسَ جَيِّدًا، لَنَجَحَ فِي الامْتِحَانِ.
concept_examples.translation: If he had studied well, he would have passed the exam.
concept_examples.phonetic: law kāna qad darasa jayyidan, la-najaḥa fī l-imtiḥān.

concept_examples.text: بَعْدَ أَنْ كَانَ قَدْ انْتَهَى مِنْ عَمَلِهِ، ذَهَبَ إِلَى النَّادِي.
concept_examples.translation: After he had finished his work, he went to the club.
concept_examples.phonetic: baʿda ʼan kāna qad intahā min ʿamalihi, ḏahaba ʼilā n-nādī.

common_error.correct_alt: كَانَ أَكَلَ الطَّعَامَ (acceptable in clear context but less emphatic)
common_error.explanation: The most common mistake is omitting 'قَدْ' after 'كَانَ' when expressing anteriority. Without 'قَدْ', the sentence 'كَانَ أَكَلَ' can be interpreted as 'he was (someone who) ate' or simply 'he ate' (simple past), losing the nuance of the past perfect. In Arabic, 'قَدْ' serves to mark that the action was already completed in the past. Spanish speakers must remember to include 'قَدْ' to avoid ambiguity.

examples.translation: He had written the letter.
examples.note: Basic structure: conjugated 'كَانَ' + 'قَدْ' + past verb.

examples.translation: I had visited Madrid.
examples.note: Conjugation of 'كَانَ' according to the subject. Here 'كُنْتُ' (kuntu) for 'I'.

examples.original: قَبْلَ أَنْ أَذْهَبَ إِلَى العَمَلِ، كَانَ قَدْ تَنَاوَلَ الفُطُورَ.
examples.phonetic: qabla ʼan ʼaḏhaba ʼilā l-ʿamali, kāna qad tanāwala l-fuṭūr.
examples.translation: Before going to work, he had already had breakfast.
examples.note: Use of 'قَبْلَ أَنْ' (before) to mark anteriority.

examples.original: بَعْدَ أَنْ كَانَ قَدْ شَاهَدَ الفِيْلْمَ، نَامَ.
examples.phonetic: baʿda ʼan kāna qad šāhada l-fīlm, nāma.
examples.translation: After he had watched the movie, he slept.
examples.note: With 'بَعْدَ أَنْ' (after) + 'كَانَ قَدْ'.

examples.original: لَوْ كَانَ قَدْ سَافَرَ، لَاكْتَشَفَ العَالَمَ.
examples.phonetic: law kāna qad sāfara, lāktašafa l-ʿālam.
examples.translation: If he had traveled, he would have discovered the world.
examples.note: Use of 'لَوْ' (if) + 'كَانَ قَدْ' + past for unreal conditions.

examples.original: لَوْ كُنْتُ قَدْ عَلِمْتُ، لَمَا فَعَلْتُ ذَلِكَ.
examples.phonetic: law kuntu qad ʿalimtu, lamā faʿaltu ḏālika.
examples.translation: If I had known, I would not have done that.
examples.note: Negation is done with 'لَمَا' + past.

title: الجمل الشرطية (النوع الأول والثاني) / Conditional sentences (Type 1 and 2)
bridge: In Arabic, conditional sentences of types 1 and 2 are distinguished not by verb tenses but by the particles used: 'إذا' (idha) for probable conditions and 'لو' (law) for improbable or hypothetical ones. A common mistake is using the present tense after 'لو' (law), which is incorrect; it should always be followed by a past tense verb (or a nominal structure). Pay attention to the particle and context rather than verb tense.
rule: Arabic conditional sentences consist of two clauses: the condition (protasis) and the result (apodosis). For type 1 (real or probable conditions), 'إذا' (idha) is used with a past or present verb, and the result can be in the present or future (e.g., إذا درستَ ستنجح / idha darasta satanjahu = If you study, you will pass). For type 2 (unreal or hypothetical conditions), 'لو' (law) is used with a past verb, and the result often includes 'كان سـ' (kana sa-) or 'لـ' (la-) + past (e.g., لو درستَ لنجحتَ / law darasta lanajalta = If you had studied, you would have passed). Unlike Spanish, Arabic does not have a clear morphological distinction between simple and compound conditionals; context determines the temporal nuance. In type 2, 'لو' (law) + past can express both hypothetical present conditions and impossible past conditions.

concept_examples.text: إذا ذهبتَ إلى السوق، اشتري خبزاً.
concept_examples.translation: If you go to the market, buy some bread.
concept_examples.phonetic: ʔiðā ðahabta ʔilā s-sūq, ištarī ḫubzan.

concept_examples.translation: If I had money, I would travel.
If you eat a lot, you will feel tired.
If I were in your place, I would do that.

common_error.wrong: لو أذهب إلى السوق، سأشتري خبزاً.
common_error.correct: لو ذهبتُ إلى السوق، لاشتريت خبزاً.
common_error.correct_alt: لو ذهبتُ إلى السوق، لاشتريت خبزاً. (or: لو كنتُ ذاهباً إلى السوق لكنتُ اشتريت خبزاً)
common_error.explanation: This error occurs because the student transfers the Spanish structure 'si + present' to Arabic by using 'لو' (law) with the present tense. In Arabic, 'لو' (law) must always be followed by a past tense verb (or a nominal structure), and the result requires the particle 'لـ' (la-) + past. To express 'if I were to go to the market' (hypothetical), use 'لو ذهبتُ' (law ðahabtu). Avoid using the present tense after 'لو' (law).

examples.translation: If you study, you will pass.
examples.note: Uses 'إذا' (idha) + past (or present) and the result with 'سـ' (future). This is the most common form for probable conditions.

examples.original: إذا كان الجو جميلاً، سنخرج في نزهة.
examples.phonetic: ʔiðā kāna l-jawwu jamīlan, sanuḫruju fī nuzhah.
examples.translation: If the weather is nice, we will go for a walk.
examples.note: Observe that the verb 'كان' (kāna) in the past describes a present/future condition.

examples.translation: If you are late, you will miss the bus.
examples.note: Here, the past 'تأخرتَ' (taʔaḫḫarta) expresses a probable future action.

levels.label: النوع الثاني: الشروط غير الواقعية (مضارع مخالف للحقيقة)
levels.translation: Type 2: Hypothetical conditions (contrary to present reality)

examples.translation: If I had time, I would help you.
examples.note: The past after 'لو' (law) expresses an unreal condition in the present. The result uses 'لـ' (la-) + past.

examples.translation: If I knew the answer, I would tell you.
examples.note: Although the past tense is typical after 'لو' (law), the present can sometimes be used (less common) to express hypothesis.

examples.original: لو كنت طائراً، لحلقت في السماء.
examples.phonetic: law kuntu ṭāʔiran, laḥallaqtu fī s-samāʔ.
examples.translation: If I were a bird, I would fly in the sky.
examples.note: With 'كان' (kāna) in the past, an impossible condition is expressed. The result in the past with 'لـ' (la-) is equivalent to the simple conditional.

levels.label: النوع الثاني: الشروط المستحيلة (ماضٍ مخالف للحقيقة)
levels.translation: Type 2: Impossible conditions (contrary to past reality)

examples.original: لو درستَ جيداً، لنجحت في الامتحان.
examples.phonetic: law darasta jayyidan, lanajaḥta fī l-imtiḥān.
examples.translation: If you had studied well, you would have passed the exam.
examples.note: Here, 'لو' (law) + past refers to an unreal past condition. The result with 'لـ' (la-) + past is equivalent to the compound conditional.

examples.translation: If it hadn’t rained, we would have gone out yesterday.
examples.note: The use of 'لم' (lam) + present (or past) after 'لو' (law) to negate the condition. The result uses 'لـ' (la-) + past.

examples.original: لو كنتُ حضرتُ الاجتماع، لاتخذنا قراراً مختلفاً.
examples.phonetic: law kuntu ḥaḍartu l-ijtimāʕ, lattāḫaḏnā qarāran muḫtalifan.
examples.translation: If I had attended the meeting, we would have made a different decision.
examples.note: The construction 'كان + اسم فاعل' (e.g., حضرتُ / ḥaḍartu = 'having attended') is used to express hypothetical past actions.

title: المبني للمجهول (presente y pasado) / Passive voice (present and past)
bridge: In Spanish, the passive voice is formed with the verb 'ser' + past participle, and the agent is introduced with 'por'. In Arabic, the passive is formed by changing the internal vowels of the verb, without needing an auxiliary verb. For Spanish-speaking students, the main challenge is getting used to the fact that the verb changes internally and that the agent is generally not mentioned. Additionally, in Arabic there is no direct equivalent of 'ser' in the passive, so you must learn to recognize the passive vowels.
rule: In Arabic, the passive voice (المبني للمجهول) is formed only by vowel changes in the verb, both in the present and past tenses. No auxiliary verb is used. For regular verbs in the past tense, the vowels change as follows: the first internal vowel (after the first consonant) becomes 'u' (ضمة) and the second vowel (after the second consonant) becomes 'i' (كسرة). For example: 'كَتَبَ' (he wrote) in the passive becomes 'كُتِبَ' (it was written). In the present tense, the vowel of the first consonant becomes 'u' (ضمة) and the following consonant carries 'a' (فتحة), but the root vowel changes to 'a' or 'i' depending on the pattern. For example: 'يَكْتُبُ' (he writes) in the passive becomes 'يُكْتَبُ' (it is written). The subject in the passive is omitted, and the verb agrees with the patient (what would be the subject in Spanish). In Arabic, the agent is not mentioned in the passive construction; if needed, another construction is used. Exceptions: verbs that begin with a vowel or hamza may have variations. Verbs in the past tense with voiceless roots may have long vowels that shorten. It is important to practice with both regular and irregular verbs.

concept_examples.translation: The lesson was written
The lesson is written
The door was opened
The door is opened

common_error.explanation: A common mistake is trying to use the agent as in Spanish with 'por' (for example, 'the book is written by Ahmed'). In Arabic, the passive does not mention the agent. Additionally, some students use the verb with a direct object in the passive, but in the passive the patient must be the grammatical subject, so it must be in the nominative case (with a final 'u') and the verb agrees with it. To mention the place or instrument, a prepositional phrase is used. So you do not say 'the book is written the writer', but rather 'يُكْتَبُ الكتابُ' (the book is written) or another structure is used.

levels.label: المبني للمجهول في الماضي
levels.translation: Passive voice in the past tense

examples.translation: The book was read
examples.note: Observe the vowel change: from قَرَأَ to قُرِئَ. The first internal vowel becomes u and the second becomes i.

examples.translation: The water was drunk
examples.note: Verb شَرِبَ (to drink) in the passive: شُرِبَ. The patient (water) becomes the subject and carries a final u.

examples.translation: The painting was drawn
examples.note: The verb agrees with the patient in gender and number: اللوحة is feminine, so the verb takes a t.

levels.label: المبني للمجهول في المضارع
levels.translation: Passive voice in the present tense

examples.translation: The lesson is written
examples.note: In the present tense, the first consonant carries a u (ضمة) and the second carries an a (فتحة). Compare with يَكْتُبُ (he writes).

examples.translation: The door is opened
examples.note: Verb فَتَحَ (to open) in the passive present: يُفْتَحُ. The root vowel changes to a.

examples.translation: The letter is written
examples.note: The verb agrees with the patient (رسالة, feminine), so it takes an initial t.

levels.label: الاستخدام مع حروف الجر وبدون ذكر الفاعل
levels.translation: Use with prepositions and without mentioning the agent

examples.translation: The book was written with the pen
examples.note: The agent is not mentioned, but the instrument is introduced with 'ب' (with).

examples.translation: The food was eaten at the restaurant
examples.note: The agent is omitted; the place is mentioned with 'في'. Observe the hamza with u in the first vowel.

examples.translation: The reason is not known
examples.note: In negation with 'لا', the passive verb is used in the same way. The patient is the subject.

title: الكلام المنقول (الأسلوب غير المباشر) / Indirect speech
bridge: In Arabic, when converting to indirect speech, we don't change the verb tenses ('he said he was tired') as we do in Spanish. Instead, we use 'أنَّ' (anna) to introduce the subordinate clause, but the verb from the original quote remains in the same tense. There is no direct equivalent to the Spanish past perfect tense. Additionally, personal and possessive pronouns are adjusted according to the speaker, similar to Spanish, but attention must be paid to gender agreement in verbs and adjectives, which also exists in Spanish but with fewer variations.
rule: To form indirect speech in Arabic, two main particles are used: 'أنَّ' (anna) for affirmative sentences and 'أنْ' (an) for subjunctive verbs (though at B1 level this is simplified). The basic structure is: communication verb (قال, أخبر, سأل) + أنَّ + subordinate clause where the subject and pronouns adjust to the speaker's perspective. The verb in the subordinate clause remains in the same tense as in direct speech (no tense changes as in Spanish). For indirect questions, 'هل' (hal) or 'إذا' (idha) is used for yes/no questions, and interrogative particles (ماذا, أين, متى, لماذا) for open-ended questions. Indirect commands are expressed with 'أنْ' + subjunctive verb. There is no change in the verbal mood in the subordinate clause, and the use of 'أنَّ' requires the subject to be in the nominative case (though this is advanced grammar; at B1 the standard form is used).

concept_examples.translation: He said he was tired.
She told me she loves reading.

concept_examples.text: سألني إذا كنت أدرس اللغة العربية.
concept_examples.translation: He asked me if I was studying Arabic.
concept_examples.phonetic: saʔalanī ʔidhā kuntu ʔadrusu al-luɣah al-ʕarabiyyah

concept_examples.text: قال لي أن أذهب إلى السوق.
concept_examples.translation: He told me to go to the market.
concept_examples.phonetic: qaːla lī ʔan ʔaðhaba ʔilā al-sūq

common_error.explanation: The most common mistake among Spanish speakers is applying Spanish logic by changing the verb tense to the past (estaba) when the main verb (قال) is already in the past. In Arabic, the verb tense in the subordinate clause remains the same as in direct speech: if the person said 'I am tired' (أنا متعب), when reporting it, you say 'he said he is tired' (قال إنه متعب). The past tense is not added. To avoid this, remember that Arabic does not have tense agreement; the context determines the time.

examples.translation: He said he is happy.
examples.note: Use 'إنَّ' to introduce an affirmative sentence. The verb 'قال' is in the past, but the subordinate clause keeps the present tense (سعيد) as it was said.

examples.translation: She told me she works in a hospital.
examples.note: 'أخبرت' (to tell) + 'أنَّ' + pronoun and verb in the present. Note that the pronoun (هي) changes to (ها) as a possessive/object pronoun.

examples.translation: They said they will travel tomorrow.
examples.note: The future is expressed with 'سـ' (sa) + present. There is no tense change, only pronouns are adjusted.

examples.translation: He asked me if I was ready.
examples.note: For yes/no questions, 'إذا' (if) is used. The verb 'كنت' is in the past because that's how it was said in direct speech ('are you ready?'), but in Arabic the original tense is kept if it is coherent.

examples.translation: I asked where you work.
examples.note: The interrogative particle 'أين' (where) is kept, and the verb is conjugated according to the new subject (you, in this case). There is no tense change.

examples.translation: I didn’t ask why he arrived late.
examples.note: 'لماذا' (why) is used the same as in Spanish. The verb 'جاء' is in the past and is not altered.

examples.translation: He asked me to wait.
examples.note: Use 'طلب' (to ask) + 'أنْ' + subjunctive verb (in Arabic, present with subjunctive ending: أنتظر). It is equivalent to 'that I wait' in Spanish.

examples.translation: He advised me to study hard.
examples.note: 'نصح' (to advise) + 'أنْ' + subjunctive. Remember that the object pronoun is 'ني' (me), but it is written as part of the verb (نصحني).

examples.translation: He ordered them to leave the room.
examples.note: 'أمر' (to order) + 'أنْ' + subjunctive. The verb 'يخرجوا' has a subjunctive ending (the final -u is omitted in subjunctive).

title: المصدر والفعل المصدري / Gerunds and Infinitives as Subject and Object
bridge: In Spanish, we use the infinitive (hablar) or the gerund (hablando) as a subject or object. In Arabic, there is no exact equivalent of the gerund; instead, the مصدر (masdar) is used, which is a verbal noun functioning as a noun. For example, 'hablar' becomes 'الكلام' (al-kalām). While Spanish often uses 'el hecho de + infinitive', in Arabic the masdar is used directly. Be careful: do not confuse the masdar with the active participle, which in Arabic indicates the agent.
rule: In Arabic, the masdar (المصدر) is a noun derived from a verb that expresses the action or state. It is used as the subject or object of a sentence. For example, 'الكلام' (al-kalām) means 'the speaking' or 'speaking'. To express 'me gusta + infinitive', the structure 'أحب + مصدر' (uḥibb + masdar) or 'يعجبني + مصدر' (yu'jibunī + masdar) is used. For 'es importante + infinitive', the structure 'من المهم + مصدر' (min al-muhimm + masdar) is used. The masdar can be definite (with 'ال') or indefinite without the article, but when it is a subject, it usually takes the article. Additionally, some verbs have irregular masdars, for example 'قال' (qaala, to say) -> 'القول' (al-qawl).

concept_examples.translation: Speaking is difficult.
I like reading.
Studying is important.
I hate waiting.

common_error.wrong: أحب أن أكل (incorrecto: usan la forma 'أن + verbo' cuando debería ser masdar)
common_error.explanation: In Spanish, we often use 'me gusta + infinitive', and in Arabic, the structure 'أن + subjunctive verb' (e.g., 'أحب أن آكل') is possible, but it is more natural and common to use the masdar. The error occurs because Spanish speakers tend to translate the infinitive literally, but they should learn to use the masdar as a noun. The 'أن' structure is grammatically correct but sounds more literal and less idiomatic.

examples.translation: Swimming is fun.
examples.note: The masdar 'السَّباحة' (as-sibāḥa) means 'swimming' or 'the act of swimming', and it functions as the subject.

examples.translation: Smoking is harmful to health.
examples.note: Observe the use of the article 'ال' in the masdar to make it definite.

examples.translation: I like traveling.
examples.note: The verb 'أحب' (uḥibb) is combined with the masdar 'السفر' (as-safar) as an object.

examples.translation: I hate noise.
examples.note: Here the masdar 'الضجيج' (aḍ-ḍajīj) is the object of 'أكره'.

examples.translation: Sleeping early is important.
examples.note: The structure 'من المهم + masdar' expresses 'it is important + infinitive'.

examples.translation: It is worth the effort.
examples.note: The masdar 'العناء' (al-ʿanāʾ) is used as the object of 'يستحق'.

translations.en: Gerunds and Infinitives as Subject and Object

title: أفعال الشك والتخمين (must, might, could) / Modal verbs for deduction
bridge: In Spanish, we use modal verbs like 'debe de', 'puede que', 'podría' to express deduction. In Arabic, this function is mainly carried out through modal particles and constructions, such as 'لابد أن' (laabudda an), 'قد' (qad), 'ربما' (rubbamaa), which are combined with verbs in the indicative or subjunctive. The key difference: in Arabic, the choice of particle indicates the degree of certainty, and there is no direct equivalent of 'must' as a modal verb; a fixed structure is used. Be careful not to translate 'must' literally with the verb 'يجب' (yajibu), which expresses obligation, not deduction.
rule:
In Arabic, the following structures are used to express deduction:
1. **High certainty (equivalent to 'must')**: 'لابد أن' (laabudda an) + verb in the present indicative (or past). Example: 'لابد أن يكون في المنزل' (laabudda an yakuuna fi al-manzil) = 'Debe de estar en casa'.
2. **Medium possibility (equivalent to 'might/could')**: 'قد' (qad) + verb in the present indicative (for future possibility) or 'قد' + verb in the past (for past possibility). Example: 'قد يأتي غداً' (qad ya'tii ghadan) = 'Puede que venga mañana'.
3. **Softer expressions of probability**: 'ربما' (rubbamaa) + verb in the indicative, similar to 'quizás' in Spanish. Example: 'ربما سافر' (rubbamaa saafara) = 'Quizás viajó'.
4. **To ask about possibility**: 'هل يمكن أن' (hal yumkin an) + subjunctive, equivalent to '¿Podría ser que...?' in Spanish.
The particles are invariable and do not change with the subject. The negative form is made with 'لا يمكن أن' (laa yumkin an) for 'no puede ser que'.
It is important to distinguish between obligation ('يجب أن' yajibu an) and deduction ('لابد أن' laabudda an), even though both are translated in Spanish as 'deber'. In deduction contexts, use 'لابد أن'.

concept_examples.text: لابد أن يكون في البيت الآن.
concept_examples.translation: He must be at home now.
concept_examples.phonetic: laabudda an yakuuna fi al-bayti al-aan

concept_examples.translation: We might go to the market tomorrow.
She might have forgotten the key in the car.

concept_examples.text: لا يمكن أن يكون هذا صحيحاً.
concept_examples.translation: It can't be that this is true.
concept_examples.phonetic: laa yumkin an yakuuna haadhaa sahiihaan

common_error.wrong: يجب أن يكون في البيت (yajibu an yakuuna fi al-bayt) – used for 'he must be at home'
common_error.correct: لابد أن يكون في البيت (laabudda an yakuuna fi al-bayt)
common_error.correct_alt: من المؤكد أنه في البيت (min al-mu'akkad annahu fi al-bayt)
common_error.explanation: The most common mistake is using 'يجب أن' (yajibu an), which means 'must' in the sense of obligation, not deduction. Spanish speakers tend to transfer the double use of 'debe' (obligation and deduction) in Spanish to Arabic, but in Arabic these are different structures. For deduction, use 'لابد أن' (laabudda an), which expresses a logical conclusion. To avoid this error, remember that 'يجب' always implies moral duty or necessity, while 'لابد' implies inferred certainty.

examples.original: لابد أنك متعب بعد الرحلة الطويلة.
examples.phonetic: laabudda annaka mut'ab ba'da al-rihlah al-tawilah
examples.translation: You must be tired after the long trip.
examples.note: Use of 'لابد أن' with the suffixed pronoun -ka to refer to the listener. The verb 'يكون' is often omitted when the predicate is an adjective.

examples.translation: They must have arrived before us.
examples.note: Here 'لابد أن' + past verb expresses a deduction about a past event.

examples.original: قد يكون الجو حاراً في الصيف.
examples.phonetic: qad yakuunu al-jawwu haarran fi al-sayf
examples.translation: It might be hot in the summer.
examples.note: When 'قد' is used with the present indicative, it indicates possibility in the present or future. It is similar to the use of 'puede que' + subjunctive in Spanish.

examples.translation: I might have forgotten our appointment.
examples.note: When 'قد' is used with a past verb, it indicates a possibility about a past event. Note that in Spanish, the present perfect or preterite is also used.

levels.label: الشك والاستفهام (ربما، هل يمكن)
levels.translation: Doubt and asking about possibility (maybe, could it be?)

examples.translation: The train might be delayed because of the weather.
examples.note: 'ربما' expresses a lower probability than 'قد' and is used with the present indicative, similar to 'quizás' + indicative in Spanish (though in Spanish the subjunctive can also be used).

examples.original: هل يمكن أن يكون هذا خطأً؟
examples.phonetic: hal yumkin an yakuuna haadhaa khata'an
examples.translation: Could this be a mistake?
examples.note: The structure 'هل يمكن أن' followed by the subjunctive is used to ask if something is possible. In Spanish, we use '¿Podría ser que...?' + subjunctive.

title: الجمل الموصولة (المعرّفة وغير المعرّفة) / Relative Clauses (Restrictive and Non-restrictive)
bridge: In Spanish, relative clauses are introduced with 'que', 'quien', 'cual', etc., and can be restrictive (without commas) or non-restrictive (with commas). In Arabic, the structure differs: a relative pronoun (الذي، التي، الذين...) agrees in gender and number with the antecedent, and the verb in the relative clause does not require an explicit relative pronoun; instead, the clause functions as a complement. A common mistake is omitting the relative pronoun when the antecedent is indefinite or using it incorrectly with definite antecedents. Additionally, in Arabic, non-restrictive relative clauses are introduced the same way as restrictive ones, but they are distinguished by pauses and context rather than commas.
rule: In Arabic, relative clauses are formed using relative pronouns that agree with the antecedent in gender, number, and case (though in Modern Standard Arabic, case is marked in the relative pronouns). The relative pronouns are: الذي (masc. sing.), التي (fem. sing.), اللذان/اللذين (masc. dual), اللتان/اللتين (fem. dual), الذين (masc. plural), اللاتي/اللوائي (fem. plural). For indefinite antecedents, the relative clause is called 'sila' and the relative pronoun is omitted; the clause is introduced directly by the verb, often translating to 'a man who...' = رجلٌ يقرأ (not رجلٌ الذي يقرأ). For definite antecedents, the relative pronoun is mandatory: الرجل الذي يقرأ. Non-restrictive (explanatory) clauses in Arabic are often set off by pauses and may be introduced the same way as restrictive ones, but sometimes constructions with 'wa' or إِذْ are used for clarification. A key point: the verb in the relative clause always agrees in gender with the antecedent, and if the antecedent is a plural non-human noun (like objects), the verb takes feminine singular agreement. Example: الكتب التي اشتريتها (the books that I bought) – the verb 'اشتريت' is in feminine singular. For B1 level, mastery of basic relative pronouns (الذي، التي، الذين، اللاتي) and their omission with indefinite antecedents is expected.

concept_examples.translation: The man who reads is my teacher.

concept_examples.text: المرأة التي تعمل في المستشفى طبيبة.
concept_examples.translation: The woman who works in the hospital is a doctor.

This is a useful book. (no relative pronoun, because it is indefinite) - Note: To say 'a book that is useful,' you could say 'هذا كتابٌ مفيدٌ' or 'هذا كتابٌ مفيدٌ جداً', but for an indefinite relative clause, you would say 'هذا كتابٌ يفيد' (this is a book that benefits).
The students who passed are happy.

common_error.wrong: الرجل الذي هو يقرأ هو أستاذي.
common_error.explanation: In Spanish, it is common to use 'que' + a personal pronoun ('que él lee'), but in Arabic, you should not add a personal pronoun after the relative pronoun. The verb already carries the person. Saying 'الذي هو يقرأ' (who he reads) is incorrect. Simply say 'الذي يقرأ' (who reads).

levels.label: الضمائر الموصولة (المذكر والمؤنث المفرد) / Relative pronouns (masculine and feminine singular)

examples.translation: This is the book that I like.
examples.note: Use of 'الذي' for masculine singular. Note that the verb 'أحب' has the suffix pronoun 'ه' referring to the book; in Spanish, this is often omitted.

examples.translation: That is the car that I bought.
examples.note: Use of 'التي' for feminine singular. The suffix 'ها' in 'اشتريتها' agrees with the car (feminine in Arabic).

examples.original: أعرف رجلاً يسكن في هذا البيت.
examples.translation: I know a man who lives in this house.
examples.note: Indefinite antecedent (رجلاً) – the relative pronoun is omitted, and the verb is used directly in the present tense.

examples.original: المعلمون الذين يدرسون في مدرستنا محبوبون.
examples.translation: The teachers who teach in our school are beloved.
examples.note: الذين for masculine plural. The verb 'يدرسون' has a plural suffix.

examples.original: الممرضات اللاتي يعملن في المستشفى مجتهدات.
examples.translation: The nurses who work in the hospital are hardworking.
examples.note: اللاتي for feminine plural. The verb 'يعملن' has a feminine plural suffix.

examples.translation: These are the books that I read.
examples.note: When the antecedent is a plural non-human noun (books), 'التي' (feminine singular) is used because it agrees as feminine singular.

levels.label: الجمل الموصولة مع تعريفات مختلفة / Relative clauses with definite and indefinite antecedents
levels.translation: Relative clauses with definite and indefinite antecedents

examples.translation: I saw a man carrying a bag.
examples.note: Indefinite antecedent: no relative pronoun is used; the relative clause is introduced directly by the verb.

examples.translation: I saw the man who is carrying a bag.
examples.note: Definite antecedent: 'الذي' is used to specify which man we are talking about.

examples.original: زوجي الذي يعمل في القاهرة يسافر كثيراً.
examples.phonetic: /zawǧī l-laðī yaʕmalu fī l-qāhirati yusāfiru kaṯīran/
examples.translation: My husband, who works in Cairo, travels a lot.
examples.note: Non-restrictive (explanatory) clause: 'الذي' is used, and it is understood from context that this is additional information; a pause is made in pronunciation.

examples.original: زوجي الذي يعمل في القاهرة يسافر كثيراً. (Sin pausa: especificativa)
examples.phonetic: /zawǧī l-laðī yaʕmalu fī l-qāhirati yusāfiru kaṯīran/
examples.translation: My husband who works in Cairo travels a lot. (Implies that I have other husbands, though this is unusual; used to specify)
examples.note: The difference between restrictive and non-restrictive clauses is not marked in writing; it depends on context and pauses.

title: التعبير عن الأمنيات غير الواقعية / Wish + past for unreal wishes
bridge: In Spanish, to express an unreal wish we use the subjunctive ('Ojalá tuviera...', 'Me gustaría que fuera...'). In Arabic, this nuance is mainly expressed with the particle 'ليت' (layta) followed by a verb in the past tense (even if the wish refers to the present or future). Another key difference is that in Arabic there is no direct equivalent of 'wish + past perfect' for wishes about the past; instead, 'ليت' with the past tense or 'يا ليت' for emphasis is used. Spanish speakers often fall into the trap of translating 'quisiera' as 'أريد' (urīdu) instead of using 'ليت'.
rule: In Arabic, to express unreal or unlikely wishes (equivalent to 'ojalá + subjunctive' or 'wish + past' in English), the particle 'ليت' (layta) is used followed by a verb in the past tense (ماضٍ) regardless of whether the wish is present or future. The basic construction is: ليت + فاعل + فعل ماضٍ. Example: ليتني أملك سيارة (laytanī amliku sayyārah) – I wish I had a car. For wishes about the past (unreal, unfulfilled), 'ليت' is used with the verb in the past perfect (كان قد + فعل) or simply the past tense, though it is common to add 'قد' to emphasize that it did not happen: ليتني قد درست أكثر (laytanī qad darastu akthar) – I wish I had studied more. Another option is 'يا ليت' for added emphasis or emotion. Note: 'ليت' is only used for possible or unreal wishes; for possible wishes that may be fulfilled, 'أتمنى' (atamannā) + present tense verb is used, similar to 'I hope that'. There is no subjunctive mood in Arabic; the past tense serves this function. In colloquial registers, it is common to use 'ليت' with the present tense as well, but in Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) the past tense is preferred. Be careful with word order: the verb agrees with the subject in gender and number.

concept_examples.translation: I wish I knew the answer.
I wish the weather were nice today.
I wish I had studied harder.
I wish we could travel now.

common_error.wrong: أريد أن أكون غنياً. (when trying to say 'I wish I were rich')
common_error.explanation: The error occurs because Spanish speakers tend to translate 'quisiera' or 'ojalá' using 'أريد' (to want) + subjunctive, but in Arabic 'أريد' expresses a real desire or will, not an unreal one. For unreal wishes, 'ليت' (or 'يا ليت') must be used with the verb in the past tense or even without a verb (with a nominal predicate). Remember: 'ليت' already implies unreality, so do not use the present tense after it in MSA.

examples.translation: I wish I were a doctor.
examples.note: When the wish is about a state or quality, 'ليت' is attached to the pronoun (ليتني = ليت + ني) and no verb is needed.

examples.translation: I wish youth would return someday.
examples.note: Here 'ليت' is followed by a noun (الشباب) and a present tense verb, but expresses an unreal wish about the future/present. This is a common poetic exception.

examples.translation: I wish the car were fast.
examples.note: A nominal predicate (سريعة) is used without a copular verb, as is typical in Arabic.

examples.translation: I wish I had listened to the advice.
examples.note: The past tense (سمعت) here expresses a wish about the past, equivalent to the pluperfect subjunctive in Spanish.

examples.translation: I wish we had arrived on time.
examples.note: The past tense is used for completed actions that did not happen, indicating regret.

examples.translation: I wish it had rained yesterday.
examples.note: In this case, the past tense refers to an unreal wish about the past.

levels.label: يا ليت و أتمنى للتمييز
levels.translation: Ya layta and atamannā for distinction

examples.translation: If only I could help you!
examples.note: The particle 'يا' before 'ليت' adds emotional emphasis, similar to 'how I wish!'.

examples.translation: I hope you pass the exam (possible wish).
examples.note: 'أتمنى' is used for possible wishes or hopes, not unreal ones. It is followed by 'أن' + verb in subjunctive/present.

examples.translation: If only time would stop!
examples.note: In colloquial or literary registers, the present tense is sometimes used after 'ليت', but in MSA the past tense (توقف) is preferred.

title: التعبير عن العادات الماضية (كان + يفعل) / Expressing Past Habits (kāna + present verb)
bridge: In Spanish, to express past habits we use the imperfect tense ('yo corría') or the periphrasis 'solía + infinitive'. In Arabic, there is no specific verb tense for this; the past form of the verb كان (kāna) 'to be' is used followed by the present form of the main verb, or the imperfect tense alone, depending on the context. Spanish speakers must be careful not to always use the simple past, since in Arabic the simple past (perfective) narrates punctual actions, not habits. Additionally, in Arabic the verb 'kāna' can be omitted in nominal sentences, but in this pattern it is essential.
rule:
In Arabic, to express habitual actions in the past (equivalent to 'solía' or 'imperfect' in Spanish), two main structures are used:

1. **كـان + فعل مضارع**: The auxiliary verb كان (kāna) is conjugated in the past (كان، كانت، كانوا...) and is followed by a verb in the present (indicative). Example: كنت أذهب (kuntu adhhabu) = 'I used to go / I went'.

2. **فعل ماضٍ فقط**: In some contexts, especially with adverbs of frequency or time, the perfective past can indicate a habit (e.g. كنا نلعب كل يوم = 'we used to play every day'), but this is less common and depends on context.

- The choice between these forms depends on emphasis: if habituality is to be emphasized, 'كان + المضارع' is preferred.
- With كان, the main verb remains in the present and does not change its form.
- The auxiliary كان agrees with the subject in gender and number.
- To negate past habits, use ما كان + مضارع (mā kāna + present) or لم + ماضٍ (lam + perfective) for general negation.
- For questions, the order is inverted or an interrogative particle is added at the beginning.
- In elevated style, the particle قد (qad) may appear before the past, but it is not necessary for habits.
- Caution: Do not confuse with the past continuous (estaba + gerund), which is expressed the same way as habits in Arabic (كان + مضارع), but the context clarifies it.

concept_examples.text: كنت أقرأ كل ليلة قبل النوم.
concept_examples.translation: I used to read every night before sleeping.
concept_examples.phonetic: kuntu aqra'u kulla laylatin qabla an-nawm.

concept_examples.text: كانوا يلعبون كرة القدم في الشارع.
concept_examples.translation: They used to play football in the street.
concept_examples.phonetic: kānū yal'abūna kurat al-qadam fī ash-shāri'.

concept_examples.text: كانت أمي تطبخ طعامًا لذيذًا كل جمعة.
concept_examples.translation: My mother used to cook delicious food every Friday.
concept_examples.phonetic: kānat ummī tabkhu ṭa'āman ladhidhan kulla jum'a.

concept_examples.text: لم أكن أفهم هذا الدرس عندما كنت صغيرًا.
concept_examples.translation: I didn’t use to understand this lesson when I was little.
concept_examples.phonetic: lam akun afham hādhā ad-dars ʿindamā kuntu ṣaghīran.

common_error.wrong: ذهبت إلى المدرسة كل يوم عندما كنت طفلًا.
common_error.correct: كنت أذهب إلى المدرسة كل يوم عندما كنت طفلًا.
common_error.correct_alt: كنت أذهب إلى المدرسة كل يوم في طفولتي.
common_error.explanation: The error comes from using the perfective past (ذهبت) instead of the auxiliary + present, because in Spanish the simple imperfect covers both uses. In Arabic, ذهبت indicates a punctual and complete action, not a habit. To express habits, you must use كان + مضارع (كنت أذهب). Practice conjugating كان with the present form of the main verb to express habituality.

examples.translation: I used to work in a store.
examples.note: Note that the verb أعمل is in the present, while كنت indicates past time.

examples.translation: He used to visit us every summer.
examples.note: Subject-verb agreement: kāna for 'he', and the present verb yazūru agrees in gender.

examples.translation: We used to play ball in the park.
examples.note: Note the use of كنا (kunnā) for 'we' and the present verb نلعب.

examples.translation: I didn’t use to drink coffee before.
examples.note: Negation is formed with 'lam' + past form of كان (أكن) + present.

examples.translation: Did you use to study French?
examples.note: In questions, 'hal' is placed at the beginning or intonation is used.

examples.original: ما كانوا يذهبون إلى السينما كثيرًا.
examples.phonetic: mā kānū yadhhabūna ilā as-sīnimā kathīran.
examples.translation: They didn’t use to go to the cinema very often.
examples.note: Also possible with 'mā' + كان + present, but 'lam' + past is more common.

levels.label: التعبير عن الاستمرارية مع الظروف الزمنية

examples.translation: It was raining all day yesterday.
examples.note: Here كان + مضارع is used to indicate an ongoing action in the past, similar to 'estaba lloviendo' in Spanish.

examples.original: كنت أتحدث مع صديقي عندما رن الهاتف.
examples.phonetic: kuntu ataḥaddathu maʿ ṣadīqī ʿindamā ranna al-hātif.
examples.translation: I was talking with my friend when the phone rang.
examples.note: The construction كان + مضارع is used for ongoing actions interrupted by another past action.

examples.original: كنا نعيش في مصر لمدة خمس سنوات.
examples.phonetic: kunnā naʿīsh fī miṣr limuddat khams sanawāt.
examples.translation: We used to live in Egypt for five years.
examples.note: Expresses a continuous situation in the past with a specific duration.

title: الغرض والسبب والنتيجة / Purpose, Cause, and Result
bridge: In Spanish we use 'para que', 'porque', 'así que' with subjunctive or indicative. In Arabic, the particles لِـ (li-) and كَيْ (kay) introduce purpose with subjunctive, while بِسَبَبِ (bisababi) expresses cause and فَـ (fa-) result. Be careful: in Arabic the verb after لِـ and كَيْ is in the subjunctive (like Spanish after 'para que'), but the particle لِـ is directly attached to the verb in the infinitive form, without explicit conjugation. Also, cause with بِسَبَبِ is followed by a noun, not a full sentence.
rule: To express purpose: use لِـ (li-) + verb in subjunctive (present form) or لِـ + infinitive (مصدر). Example: ذَهَبْتُ لِأَتَعَلَّمَ (I went to learn). Alternative: كَيْ (kay) + subjunctive, more formal. For cause: بِسَبَبِ + noun (because of), or لِأَنَّ + sentence (because). For result: فَـ (fa-) + sentence indicating consequence, or لِذٰلِكَ (therefore), وَلٰذٰلِكَ. At B1 level, it is expected to use لِـ with the subjunctive correctly, avoiding the indicative. Note: لِـ merges with the verb and is not separated. The negation of purpose is done with لِكَيْ لَا (so as not to) or لِئَلَّا.

concept_examples.translation: I study to pass the exam.
I arrived late because of the traffic.
It rained, so the party was canceled.
I drink coffee to wake up.

common_error.explanation: The typical mistake is using لِأَنَّ (because) instead of لِـ (to) when expressing purpose. لِأَنَّ introduces a cause, not a purpose. Additionally, you should not add أَنَّ after لِـ. For purpose, we use لِـ directly attached to the verb in the subjunctive, or كَيْ + subjunctive. Remember: لِـ for purpose, لِأَنَّ for cause.

examples.translation: I use the computer for work.
examples.note: لِـ + infinitive (مصدر) is common for purpose without a verb.

examples.translation: We use the app to learn.
examples.note: لِـ + verb in subjunctive (present form). Note that the final vowel changes to -a.

examples.original: هِيَ تَتَكَلَّمُ بِصَوْتٍ عَالٍ لِيَسْمَعَهَا الْجَمِيعُ.
examples.phonetic: hiya tatakallamu biṣawtin ʕālin liyasmaʕahā l-jamīʕ.
examples.translation: She speaks loudly so that everyone can hear her.
examples.note: With suffixed pronoun: لِ + يَسْمَعَ + ها = لِيَسْمَعَها.

examples.original: لَمْ أَذْهَبْ إِلَى الْعَمَلِ بِسَبَبِ الْمَرَضِ.
examples.phonetic: lam ʔaðhab ʔilā l-ʕamali bisababi l-maraḍ.
examples.translation: I didn’t go to work because of the illness.
examples.note: بِسَبَبِ + noun, not a sentence. Equivalent to 'due to'.

examples.translation: I learned Arabic because it is a beautiful language.
examples.note: لِأَنَّ + sentence (subject + predicate). Here لِأَنَّ functions like 'because'.

examples.translation: I traveled because of work.
examples.note: Common form: بِسَبَبِ + noun, without a verb.

examples.translation: I got tired, so I rested.
examples.note: فَـ + sentence indicates an immediate result or consequence.

examples.translation: It’s raining, therefore I took the umbrella.
examples.note: لِذٰلِكَ (therefore) is more formal than فَـ.

examples.translation: He studied a lot, so he passed.
examples.note: فَنَجَحَ: فَ + نَجَحَ (he passed) – direct result.
